question: How do fine-tuning, reinforcement learning and test-time scaling fit together as post-training methods that improve reasoning, alignment and efficiency in LLMs?
contributions: A comprehensive and systematic review of post-training methodologies for LLMs, covering fine-tuning, RL and scaling as integral components of model optimization.
A structured taxonomy of post-training techniques, with open challenges and future directions.
Practical guidance through key benchmarks, datasets and evaluation metrics.

limits: Survey with no experiments: every number is quoted from other work, and several (94% MATH, 22% wasted compute, 18% latency, 29% forgetting, r=0.34) have no traceable source or setup.

Citation errors: DPO is cited as [162] (Guo et al. 2024, online AI feedback) rather than Rafailov et al. [57] in Secs 3.2.6 and the Sec 3 intro; overthinking is cited to [373], a survey of personal LLM agents; one citation prints as [?].

Terminology slips: 'Policy Reward Modeling (PRM)' is used where Process Reward Model is meant (Sec 3.1.4 callout); ORPO is described by a pairwise odds loss that omits its reference-free SFT term; the DPO loss is printed without the negative log.

Table 1 lists DeepSeek-R1 as 240B-A22B and Chinchilla and Grok3 with RL methods that the original reports do not describe in that way, so Table 1 should not be used as a source for parameter counts or training recipes.
Fig 7 trend analysis gives no search protocol or paper counts; the corpus of 'all papers' is not defined.
Covers work up to early 2025 (v2, 24 Mar 2025); later RL-for-reasoning work (RLVR variants, DAPO and others) is absent.
practices: Run LLM RL as SFT, then reward-model training on preferences, then policy-gradient fine-tuning with a KL penalty to the base model (Sec 3, 3.2.2).
Use a KL penalty beta*KL(pi||rho) during PPO to stop over-optimisation of the proxy reward (Sec 3.2.2).
Prefer GRPO when memory is tight: group-normalised rewards remove the critic (Sec 3.2.8).
Use process rewards for math, legal and code tasks where the path matters, outcome rewards for short answers; the two can be combined (Sec 3.1.3-3.1.4).
Refresh the reward model iteratively to counter reward hacking and drift (Sec 3.1.5).
Filter DPO training data by perplexity under the reference model, keeping responses under about the 95th percentile (Sec 3.2.6).
Seed RL with a small cold-start set of CoT examples, then rejection-sample and SFT, then a second RL stage for alignment, then distil (Sec 3.3).
Pick the test-time strategy by difficulty: beam search with PRM or revisions for hard prompts at low budget, best-of-N for easy ones (Sec 5.2-5.3).
Use PEFT (LoRA, QLoRA) with quantization for cheap fine-tuning on limited hardware (Sec 4.7).
Use test-time scaling when the base model is already competent and the budget is flexible; use pretraining for new capabilities (Sec 5.13).

terms.definition: multiple rounds of fine-tuning and alignment after next-token pretraining that mitigate LLM limitations by refining behavior and aligning outputs with human intent
A(s, a) = Q(s, a) - V(s): how much better or worse it is to take action a in state s compared to the baseline V(s)
measures the end result, for example whether the final answer is correct
assigns feedback at intermediate reasoning steps
explicit rewards come from rules, heuristics or human annotations; implicit rewards are inferred from interaction signals such as upvotes or click-through
generate N candidates and pick the best by a reward model or likelihood; an application of rejection sampling with N the only inference parameter
enhancing reasoning during inference, typically without model updates
sample diverse reasoning chains and choose the most consistent final answer by majority vote
categorise prompts into five difficulty levels and allocate sequential refinement or parallel search accordingly
ability to generate logically coherent responses based on statistical patterns in data rather than explicit logical inference or symbolic manipulation
